nameStory: Lance-leaved Coreopsis gets its name from its narrow, pointed leaves that resemble the tip of a lance or spear. The genus name 'Coreopsis' comes from Greek words meaning 'bug-like,' referring to the small, dark seeds that supposedly look like tiny insects. Many people know this plant better by its other common name, 'tickseed,' because the seeds are said to resemble small ticks!
description: Lance-leaved Coreopsis is a cheerful wildflower that brightens meadows and roadsides with its golden-yellow, daisy-like blooms. This native perennial grows 1-3 feet tall with narrow, lance-shaped leaves and produces abundant flowers from late spring through summer. Each flower has eight bright yellow petals with distinctively notched tips, creating a scalloped edge around a darker yellow center. It's a hardy, drought-tolerant plant that spreads by underground stems to form colonies of sunny blooms.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers about 2 inches across with exactly 8 petals, each with 3-4 deep notches at the tip creating a scalloped or tooth-like edge. The center is darker yellow and feels slightly rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth and are widest near the middle, tapering to pointed tips. Lower leaves may have a few small lobes, while upper leaves are usually smooth-edged and clasp the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple flowering stems rising from the base. Plants often spread to create patches through underground runners, with stems that feel sturdy but not woody.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, flattened seeds that are oval-shaped and feel papery. They lack the feathery bristles of dandelion seeds but may have tiny scales that help them stick to clothing and fur.

habitat: Lance-leaved Coreopsis thrives in sunny, open areas with well-drained soils, including meadows, prairies, roadsides, and disturbed sites throughout New England. It's particularly common in sandy or rocky soils and can tolerate drought conditions once established. You'll often find it growing alongside other sun-loving wildflowers like Black-eyed Susan and Wild Bergamot in old fields and grasslands.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of narrow leaves close to the ground. Flower buds begin forming on tall stems in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant bright yellow flowers from June through August. Seeds begin developing in late summer as older flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue blooming into early fall while seeds ripen and disperse. Leaves begin to yellow and die back with the first frosts.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only underground stems and roots. Look for dried seed heads on old stems that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Lance-leaved Coreopsis flowers are actually not single flowers at all, but dozens of tiny individual flowers packed together! What looks like yellow 'petals' are actually entire flowers called ray flowers, while the center contains hundreds of tiny tube flowers - it's like a botanical apartment building with hundreds of residents all living under one roof.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Black-eyed Susan, but Coreopsis has notched petal tips (like tiny teeth) while Black-eyed Susan has smooth, unnotched petals. Memory trick: 'Coreopsis has cuts' - remember the notched petals that look like they've been cut with scissors.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tickseed,' this plant has nothing to do with actual ticks and won't attract them to your garden. The name simply refers to the seed's appearance. This native wildflower is beloved by gardeners and is the state wildflower of Florida, though our New England populations represent the northern edge of its natural range.
compareHints: Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves. Large-flowered Tickseed is very similar but typically has broader leaves and slightly larger flowers, making field identification between these two quite challenging.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers.
Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem.
Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group.
Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall.

Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem.

Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis.

Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable.
